course.title: SQL and Databases
course.tagline: Query, design and manage databases with SQL, from your first SELECT to real reports.

days.title: What a Database Is and How to Set One Up
days.goal: Understand what a database is and install a free one on your computer.

video.title: SQL and Databases - A Full Course for Beginners

steps: Install MySQL or PostgreSQL on your computer, or use an online SQL playground.
Open the database tool and connect to your local server.
Make a database called practice with CREATE DATABASE practice;.
Use the database with USE practice; and check it is selected.
days.task: Set up your database and create a database called practice.
days.challenge: List the databases on your server to confirm yours is there.

options: A organised store for data that many programs can read and update safely
quiz.explain: A database stores data in an organised way so programs can find, add, change and delete it safely.

options: Structured Query Language: the language you use to ask a database for data
quiz.explain: SQL is the language for talking to databases: asking questions, adding data and changing it.

options: A set of rows and columns that stores one kind of thing, like customers
quiz.explain: A table stores one kind of data. Each row is one item, each column is one fact about it.

days.title: Your First Table
days.goal: Create a table with columns and the right data types.

video.title: Mastering SQL for Web Developers – Full Course

steps: Create a table called customers with id, name, email and city columns.
Choose the right type for each column: INT for id, VARCHAR for text.
Make id the primary key so each row has a unique number.
Show the table's structure to check your columns are right.
days.task: Create a customers table with at least five columns and a primary key.
days.challenge: Create a second table called orders with order id, customer id and amount.

options: A column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each row
quiz.explain: A primary key gives each row a unique value, so you can always tell rows apart.

options: A text type that can hold up to 100 characters
quiz.explain: VARCHAR stores text. The number sets the longest text it can hold.

quiz.q: Why choose the right data type?
options: So the database stores data correctly and can check it, like rejecting text in a number column
quiz.explain: Types tell the database what each column holds, so it can store it right and catch mistakes.

days.title: Inserting Data
days.goal: Add rows to a table with INSERT.

video.title: Learn Relational Database Design

steps: Insert one customer with INSERT INTO customers VALUES (...).
Insert three more customers in one statement.
Insert a row naming only some columns and let the rest be empty.
Check your rows with SELECT * FROM customers;.
days.task: Add ten customers to your table with realistic names, emails and cities.
days.challenge: Add five orders linked to your customers by their id.

options: It adds new rows to a table
quiz.explain: INSERT INTO adds new rows to a table with the values you give.

quiz.q: Why name the columns in an INSERT?
options: So the values go into the right columns even if the table changes
quiz.explain: Naming columns makes your intent clear and protects you if the table order changes.

quiz.q: What happens if you skip a column with no default?
options: It gets NULL (empty) unless the column forbids it
quiz.explain: A skipped column gets NULL unless it is defined as NOT NULL, which would cause an error.

days.title: Your First SELECT
days.goal: Read data back with SELECT and pick the columns you want.

video.title: Learn SQL for Analytics

steps: Run SELECT * FROM customers; to see every row and column.
Run SELECT name, city FROM customers; to see only two columns.
Run SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers; to see each city once.
Count the rows with SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers;.
days.task: Write queries that show all customers, then only names and emails, then each city once.
days.challenge: Count how many customers are in each city.

options: It returns every column of every row
quiz.explain: SELECT * returns all columns. It is handy for a quick look, but name your columns in real work.

options: It removes duplicate values so each value appears once
quiz.explain: DISTINCT removes duplicates from the result, so each value shows only once.
COUNT(*) counts the rows in the result.

days.title: Filtering with WHERE
days.goal: Filter rows with WHERE and comparison operators.

video.title: Learn Databases and SQL from Harvard University

steps: Find customers in Lagos with WHERE city = 'Lagos'.
Find orders over 10000 with WHERE amount > 10000.
Combine two conditions with AND.
Find customers in Lagos or Abuja with OR.
days.task: Find all orders over 5000 made in the last month.
days.challenge: Find all customers whose name starts with A using LIKE 'A%'.

options: It filters rows, keeping only those that match a condition
quiz.explain: WHERE keeps only the rows where the condition is true.

options: It finds values that start with A
It finds values that end with A
quiz.explain: LIKE with % matches patterns. 'A%' means the value starts with A.

quiz.q: What is the difference between AND and OR?
options: AND needs both conditions true, OR needs at least one true
quiz.explain: AND keeps rows where both conditions are true. OR keeps rows where at least one is true.

days.title: Sorting and Limiting
days.goal: Sort results with ORDER BY and limit how many rows you get.

video.title: Learn SQL for Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval

steps: Sort customers by name from A to Z with ORDER BY name.
Sort orders by amount from biggest to smallest with ORDER BY amount DESC.
Show only the top 5 orders with LIMIT 5.
Sort by city first, then by name inside each city.
days.task: List the top 10 biggest orders and the 10 smallest.
days.challenge: Show the five most recent orders by date.

options: It sorts the result rows by a column
quiz.explain: ORDER BY sorts the results by the column you name.
DESC sorts descending: biggest first. ASC (the default) sorts ascending: smallest first.

options: It returns only the first five rows of the result
quiz.explain: LIMIT caps how many rows you get back, which is handy for top-N lists.

days.title: Project 1: Build a Small Database
days.goal: Build a small database for a shop: customers, products and orders.

video.title: SQL JOINs Explained with Real Business Data

steps: Design three tables: customers, products and orders, with the right columns.
Make id the primary key in each table.
Add at least 10 customers, 10 products and 20 orders.
Write five queries that answer real questions about your shop.
days.task: Finish the shop database and run your five queries to check they work.
days.challenge: Add a fourth table for categories and link products to it.

quiz.q: What should you design before creating tables?
options: The tables, their columns, types and how they link together
quiz.explain: Design first: what tables you need, what each holds, and how they connect. It saves painful fixes later.

quiz.q: Why link orders to customers by id?
options: So each order points to exactly one customer and you can join them later
quiz.explain: Linking by id connects the tables. You can then join them to see who ordered what.

quiz.q: How do you check your database works?
options: Run queries that answer real questions and check the answers make sense
quiz.explain: Real queries that return sensible answers prove your tables and data are right.

project.title: Build a Small Shop Database
project.brief: Design and build a small database for a shop: customers, products and orders tables with primary keys, at least 10 customers, 10 products and 20 orders, plus five queries that answer real questions about the shop.
checks: Three tables exist: customers, products and orders.
Each table has a primary key.
The tables hold at least 10 customers, 10 products and 20 orders.
Orders link to customers by id.
Five queries answer real questions about the shop.
Every query runs without errors.

days.title: Updating and Deleting Data
days.goal: Change rows with UPDATE and remove them with DELETE, safely.

video.title: What a Table Is and Your First SELECT | Six Minutes: SQL, Part 1

steps: Change one customer's city with UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE ...;.
Update several rows at once with a condition.
Delete one row with DELETE FROM ... WHERE ...;.
Always check your WHERE clause first with a SELECT before updating or deleting.
days.task: Update the price of three products and delete one order that was cancelled.
days.challenge: Practise the safety habit: run the SELECT version of your WHERE first.

quiz.q: Why must UPDATE always have a WHERE?
options: Without WHERE it changes every row in the table
quiz.explain: An UPDATE without WHERE changes all rows. A WHERE limits it to the rows you mean.

quiz.q: Why check with SELECT before a DELETE?
options: So you see exactly which rows will be deleted before they are gone
quiz.explain: A SELECT with the same WHERE shows you the rows at risk. Deleting is hard to undo.

quiz.q: What does SET do in an UPDATE?
options: It names the new value for a column
quiz.explain: SET assigns the new value to the column you are updating.

days.title: Aggregate Functions
days.goal: Summarise data with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX.

video.title: Learn SQL for Data Analysis in one hour

steps: Count all orders with COUNT(*).
Find total sales with SUM(amount).
Find the average order value with AVG(amount).
Find the biggest and smallest order with MAX() and MIN().
days.task: Calculate total sales, average order value, biggest order and number of orders in your shop.
days.challenge: Find the average price of products in each category.

options: It adds up all the values in the amount column
quiz.explain: SUM adds all the values in a column together into one total.

options: It calculates the average of the values
quiz.explain: AVG adds the values and divides by how many there are, giving the average.

quiz.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
options: COUNT(*) counts all rows, COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not empty
quiz.explain: COUNT(*) counts every row. COUNT(column) skips rows where that column is NULL.

days.title: Grouping with GROUP BY
days.goal: Group rows and calculate per group with GROUP BY.

video.title: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners

steps: Count orders per customer with GROUP BY customer_id.
Find total sales per city with GROUP BY city.
Filter groups with HAVING, like only cities with more than 5 orders.
Sort the groups by their total sales.
days.task: Find total sales and order count for each product category.
days.challenge: Find which city has the highest average order value.

options: It splits rows into groups by a column's values so you can calculate per group
quiz.explain: GROUP BY makes one group per value, like one group per city, then aggregates run on each group.

quiz.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after grouping
quiz.explain: WHERE filters individual rows first. HAVING filters the groups that result, like 'only groups with more than 5 orders'.

quiz.q: Why must SELECT columns be in GROUP BY or an aggregate?
options: Because each group produces one row, so every value shown must be per group
quiz.explain: A grouped query returns one row per group. A column that is not grouped or aggregated has no single value per group.

days.title: Working with Dates and Text
days.goal: Work with dates and text functions in SQL.

video.title: SQL and Databases - A Full Course for Beginners

steps: Filter orders from the last 30 days with a date condition.
Extract the year and month from a date column.
Use UPPER() and LOWER() to change text case.
Use CONCAT() to join first and last name into a full name.
days.task: Find all orders from this month and show the customer's full name for each.
days.challenge: Find customers whose email ends with '@gmail.com'.

quiz.q: How do you compare dates in SQL?
options: With the same operators: = < > and BETWEEN for a range
quiz.explain: Dates compare like numbers. BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31' finds a whole month.

options: It joins two or more text values into one
quiz.explain: CONCAT sticks text values together, like joining a first name and a last name.

options: It turns text into capital letters
quiz.explain: UPPER() returns the text in capitals. LOWER() returns it in small letters.

days.title: Handling NULL Values
days.goal: Understand NULL and handle missing data in queries.

video.title: Mastering SQL for Web Developers – Full Course

steps: Find rows where email is NULL with WHERE email IS NULL.
Find rows where email is not empty with WHERE email IS NOT NULL.
Replace NULL with a default using COALESCE() or IFNULL().
Count how many rows have a missing phone number.
days.task: Find all customers with no phone number and fill in 'Not given' in your report query.
days.challenge: Count missing values in each column of your orders table.

options: A missing value: we do not have this information
quiz.explain: NULL means missing or unknown. It is not zero and not an empty string.

quiz.q: Why use IS NULL instead of = NULL?
options: = NULL never matches anything, because NULL is not equal to anything, even itself
quiz.explain: NULL is not a value, so = cannot compare it. IS NULL is the correct test.

options: It returns the first value that is not NULL, or a default you choose
quiz.explain: COALESCE picks the first non-NULL value in its list, so you can show a default like 'Not given'.

days.title: JOINs: Combining Tables
days.goal: Combine rows from two tables with INNER JOIN.

video.title: Learn Relational Database Design

steps: Join orders to customers to show who placed each order.
Join orders to products to show what was ordered.
Use table aliases like c and o to keep queries short.
Join three tables in one query: orders, customers and products.
days.task: Write a query that lists each order with the customer name, product name and amount.
days.challenge: Find orders with no matching customer (if any) and explain why.

options: It combines rows from two tables where the link matches
quiz.explain: INNER JOIN pairs rows from two tables where the join condition matches, like order.customer_id = customer.id.

options: A short name for a table in a query, like c for customers
quiz.explain: An alias is a nickname for a table in one query, so you can write c.name instead of customers.name.

quiz.q: What is ON in a JOIN?
options: A filter for the final result
The condition that says how rows from the two tables match
quiz.explain: ON states the link between the tables, usually that a foreign key equals a primary key.

days.title: Project 2: Sales Report with JOINs
days.goal: Build a sales report that joins tables and answers business questions.

video.title: Learn SQL for Analytics

steps: Use your shop database with customers, products and orders.
Write a query for total sales per product with a JOIN and GROUP BY.
Write a query for total sales per customer.
Write a query for the best-selling product in each city.
days.task: Finish the sales report with at least four queries and write one sentence for each finding.
days.challenge: Add a query that finds customers who have never ordered.

quiz.q: What makes a good report query?
options: It answers one clear question with a number
quiz.explain: A good report query answers one question and returns a number you can act on.

quiz.q: Why join tables for a report?
options: Because the facts you need live in different tables
quiz.explain: Customers, products and orders live in separate tables. JOINs bring them together for one answer.

quiz.q: How do you find customers who never ordered?
options: With a LEFT JOIN and a check for NULL on the order side
quiz.explain: A LEFT JOIN keeps all customers, and rows with no order have NULL order values, which you can filter for.

project.title: Sales Report with JOINs
project.brief: Build a sales report on your shop database using JOINs and GROUP BY: total sales per product, total sales per customer, best-selling product per city, and customers who have never ordered.
checks: A query shows total sales per product using a JOIN.
A query shows total sales per customer.
A query shows the best-selling product in each city.
A query finds customers who have never ordered.
Each finding has one sentence explaining what it means.
Every query runs without errors.

days.title: LEFT, RIGHT and FULL JOINs
days.goal: Keep unmatched rows with LEFT, RIGHT and FULL JOINs.

video.title: Learn Databases and SQL from Harvard University

steps: Use LEFT JOIN to show all customers, even those with no orders.
Find customers with no orders by checking for NULL on the order side.
Try RIGHT JOIN and compare the result with LEFT JOIN.
Use UNION to combine two result sets into one list.
days.task: List all customers with their order count, including customers with zero orders.
days.challenge: Combine a list of customer emails and supplier emails into one list with UNION.

options: It keeps all rows from the left table, even when there is no match on the right
quiz.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps every left row. Rows with no match get NULL for the right table's columns.

options: It stacks the results of two queries into one list, removing duplicates
quiz.explain: UNION combines two result sets with the same columns into one, with duplicates removed.

quiz.q: When would you use a LEFT JOIN instead of an INNER JOIN?
options: When you need all rows from one side, even those with no match
quiz.explain: Use LEFT JOIN when missing matches still matter, like customers who have not ordered yet.

days.title: Subqueries
days.goal: Use a query inside another query to answer harder questions.

video.title: Learn SQL for Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval

steps: Find products that cost more than the average price with a subquery.
Find customers who ordered more than the average order count.
Use a subquery in the WHERE clause with IN.
Use a subquery in the SELECT to show a value beside each row.
days.task: Find all products that sold more than the average product's total sales.
days.challenge: Find the customer with the highest total spending using a subquery.

options: A query inside another query, in brackets, that returns a value or a set of rows
quiz.explain: A subquery runs inside an outer query and gives it a value or a list to compare against.

quiz.q: What does WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products) do?
options: It keeps products that cost more than the average price
quiz.explain: The subquery calculates the average price, and the outer query keeps products above it.

quiz.q: When is a subquery better than a JOIN?
options: When you need a single value or a simple filter, a subquery can be clearer
quiz.explain: For a single comparison value, a subquery is often simpler to read than a join.

days.title: Window Functions
days.goal: Rank and compare rows with window functions like ROW_NUMBER and RANK.

video.title: SQL JOINs Explained with Real Business Data

steps: Rank products by sales with RANK() OVER (ORDER BY sales DESC).
Number rows in each category with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sales DESC).
Show each order beside the running total with SUM() OVER (ORDER BY date).
Compare each order with the previous one using LAG().
days.task: Rank your products by total sales and show the top 3 in each category.
days.challenge: Show a running total of sales over time.

options: It defines the window of rows a function looks at, without collapsing them
quiz.explain: OVER defines the window. Unlike GROUP BY, it keeps every row and adds a calculated value beside it.

options: It splits rows into groups, like GROUP BY, but keeps each row
quiz.explain: PARTITION BY divides rows into groups. The function runs separately in each group.

quiz.q: What is the difference between RANK() and ROW_NUMBER()?
options: RANK gives the same rank to ties and skips numbers, ROW_NUMBER gives every row a unique number
quiz.explain: RANK shares ranks for equal values and skips the next numbers. ROW_NUMBER never shares.

days.title: Indexes and Performance
days.goal: Make queries fast with indexes and check how they run.

video.title: What a Table Is and Your First SELECT | Six Minutes: SQL, Part 1

steps: Add an index on a column you filter often, like email or city.
Run a query before and after adding the index and compare the time.
Use EXPLAIN to see how the database runs your query.
Remove an index you do not need with DROP INDEX.
days.task: Add indexes to the columns your report queries filter and join on, then test the speed.
days.challenge: Use EXPLAIN on your slowest query and write down what it shows.

options: A lookup structure that helps the database find rows fast, like a book's index
quiz.explain: An index lets the database jump straight to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table.

quiz.q: When should you add an index?
options: On columns you often filter, join or sort by
quiz.explain: Indexes speed up searches on the columns they cover, but they slow down writes, so add them where they help.

options: It shows the plan the database will use to run your query
quiz.explain: EXPLAIN shows how the database will execute your query, including whether it uses an index.

days.title: Database Design: Normalisation
days.goal: Design clean tables with normalisation: one fact, one place.

video.title: Learn SQL for Data Analysis in one hour

steps: Spot repeated data in a flat table, like the same customer name on every order.
Split it into two tables linked by an id.
Check that each table has one job and no repeated facts.
Draw a simple diagram of your tables and their links.
days.task: Redesign a messy flat table into two or three clean tables.
days.challenge: Check your shop database: does any fact appear in two places?

options: Organising tables so each fact lives in one place and is not repeated
quiz.explain: Normalisation removes repeated data by splitting tables, so a change in one place updates everywhere.

quiz.q: What problem does repeated data cause?
options: If you update one copy and miss another, the data disagrees with itself
quiz.explain: Repeated data can get out of sync. One copy says Lagos, another says Abuja, and you no longer know the truth.

options: A column that points to the primary key of another table, linking the two
quiz.explain: A foreign key stores another table's primary key, which is how tables link together.

days.title: Relationships: One-to-Many and Many-to-Many
days.goal: Model real relationships between tables correctly.

video.title: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners

steps: Model one-to-many: one customer has many orders, using a foreign key.
Model many-to-many: students and courses, using a join table.
Create the join table with two foreign keys as its primary key.
Query across the join table to list each student's courses.
days.task: Add a many-to-many relationship to your shop: products and tags, with a join table.
days.challenge: List each product with its tags using two JOINs.

options: One row in table A links to many rows in table B, like one customer with many orders
quiz.explain: One-to-many means one parent row has many child rows, linked by a foreign key on the child.

options: One row links to one row
Rows on both sides can link to many rows on the other side, like students and courses
quiz.explain: Many-to-many means each student takes many courses and each course has many students.

options: A small table with two foreign keys that links two tables in a many-to-many relationship
quiz.explain: A join table holds one row per link, with a foreign key to each side.

days.title: Project 3: Complete Reporting Database
days.goal: Build a complete reporting database with clean design, views and a report.

video.title: SQL and Databases - A Full Course for Beginners

steps: Design a database for a small business with at least four tables and a many-to-many link.
Create the tables with primary and foreign keys.
Add realistic data: at least 20 rows in the main tables.
Build two views and write a report with five queries that answer business questions.
days.task: Finish the reporting database, views and report, and check every query runs.
days.challenge: Add an index to the columns your report filters on.

quiz.q: What makes a database design complete?
options: Clean tables, correct links, realistic data and queries that answer real questions
quiz.explain: A complete design has clean tables, correct relationships, realistic data and useful queries.

quiz.q: Why build views for a report?
options: So the report queries stay short and readable
quiz.explain: Views hide the long joins, so each report query is short and clear.

quiz.q: How do you know your report is good?
options: Each query answers one real question and the numbers make sense
quiz.explain: A good report answers real questions with numbers that check out against the data.

project.title: Complete Reporting Database
project.brief: Build a complete reporting database for a small business with at least four tables and a many-to-many link, realistic data, two views, and a report with five queries that answer business questions.
checks: The database has at least four tables with primary and foreign keys.
It includes a many-to-many relationship with a join table.
The main tables hold realistic data (at least 20 rows).
Two views exist and can be queried like tables.
The report has five queries that answer business questions.
Every query runs without errors.

days.title: Views
days.goal: Save useful queries as views so you can reuse them.

video.title: Mastering SQL for Web Developers – Full Course

steps: Create a view that shows each order with customer and product names.
Query the view like a table with SELECT * FROM order_details.
Update the underlying data and check the view shows the new data.
Drop a view you no longer need.
days.task: Make a view for your best-selling products report and query it.
days.challenge: Make a view that shows monthly sales totals.

options: A saved query that behaves like a table but stores no data of its own
quiz.explain: A view is a saved SELECT. You query it like a table, and it runs the saved query each time.

options: To reuse a complex query without rewriting it, and to hide complexity
quiz.explain: Views save you rewriting long joins. They also let you share a simple view while hiding the messy details.

options: No, it runs its saved query each time you use it
quiz.explain: A view stores only the query, not the data. The data is read fresh from the real tables each time.

days.title: Stored Procedures and Functions
days.goal: Save reusable logic in the database with stored procedures.

video.title: Learn Relational Database Design

steps: Write a stored procedure that adds a new order for a customer.
Call it with different values and check the rows appear.
Write a function that calculates the total spent by one customer.
Call the function inside a SELECT.
days.task: Write a procedure that records a sale and updates the product stock.
days.challenge: Write a function that returns the average order value for a customer.

options: A saved set of SQL statements you can call by name with values
quiz.explain: A stored procedure is a saved routine in the database. You call it by name instead of repeating the SQL.

options: To reuse logic, keep it in one place and make sure every caller does it the same way
quiz.explain: Procedures keep logic in one place. Every app that calls it gets the same behaviour.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a procedure and a function?
options: A function returns a value you can use in a query, a procedure runs steps and may return nothing
quiz.explain: A function returns a value, so you can use it inside a SELECT. A procedure runs a set of steps.

days.title: Transactions and Data Safety
days.goal: Keep data correct with transactions: all or nothing.

video.title: Learn SQL for Analytics

steps: Start a transaction, insert two related rows, then COMMIT.
Start another, insert a bad row, then ROLLBACK and check nothing changed.
Move money between two accounts in one transaction so it never half-happens.
Explain in plain words why a bank transfer must be a transaction.
days.task: Write a transaction that records an order and reduces stock, and test the rollback.
days.challenge: Try a transaction with a deliberate error and confirm nothing was saved.

options: A group of changes that succeed together or fail together
quiz.explain: A transaction wraps several changes. Either all of them happen, or none of them do.

options: It saves the transaction's changes permanently
quiz.explain: COMMIT makes the transaction's changes permanent.

options: It undoes all changes in the current transaction
quiz.explain: ROLLBACK throws away the transaction's changes, leaving the data as it was.

days.title: Backups and Security Basics
days.goal: Protect your data with backups and sensible access control.

video.title: Learn Databases and SQL from Harvard University

steps: Export your database to a backup file.
Delete a table, then restore it from the backup.
Create a read-only user for reports and test that they cannot delete data.
Write down a simple backup schedule: what to back up and how often.
days.task: Back up your shop database, test the restore, and write your backup plan.
days.challenge: Create a user who can only read data and test it.

options: Because hardware fails and mistakes happen, and a backup is the only way to get data back
quiz.explain: Without a backup, a deleted table or a failed disk means the data is gone forever.

options: An export of the database to a file you store somewhere safe
quiz.explain: An export dumps the whole database to a file. You can restore from it later.

quiz.q: Why give report users read-only access?
options: So a report can never change or delete data by mistake
quiz.explain: Read-only access means reports can never damage data, even if a query has a mistake.

days.title: SQL in Real Applications
days.goal: See how apps use SQL: connecting, querying and keeping data safe.

video.title: Learn SQL for Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval

steps: Connect a small Python script to your database and run a SELECT.
Use a parameter in the query instead of pasting values into the SQL text.
Explain in plain words what SQL injection is and why parameters stop it.
List the tables your app would need for a simple shop.
days.task: Write a Python script that connects to your database and prints the top 5 products.
days.challenge: Rewrite a query with a parameter and test it with a tricky input like a quote mark.

options: An attack where a user types SQL into a form and the app runs it, letting them read or delete data
quiz.explain: SQL injection happens when user input is pasted into SQL text. A crafted input can change the query and steal or destroy data.

quiz.q: How do parameters stop SQL injection?
options: They send the value separately from the SQL, so the database treats it as data, never as code
quiz.explain: Parameters keep code and data apart. The database never runs a value as SQL.

quiz.q: Why should apps never build SQL by joining strings?
options: Because a single quote in the input can break the query or turn it into an attack
quiz.explain: Joining strings mixes data with code. One quote can break the query or open the door to injection.

days.title: Triggers
days.goal: Make the database react automatically with triggers.

video.title: SQL JOINs Explained with Real Business Data

steps: Create a trigger that logs every new order into an audit table.
Make a trigger that updates product stock when an order is inserted.
Test the trigger by inserting an order and checking the stock.
Drop a trigger you no longer need.
days.task: Add a trigger that records every price change in a price history table.
days.challenge: Add a trigger that stops an order when the stock is zero.

options: Code the database runs automatically when a row is inserted, updated or deleted
quiz.explain: A trigger fires on a data change. It can log the change, update another table or block a bad change.

quiz.q: Why log changes with a trigger?
options: So you have a history of who changed what and when
quiz.explain: An audit log from triggers shows every change, which helps you find mistakes and prove what happened.

quiz.q: When should you be careful with triggers?
options: When they hide important logic where developers cannot see it, making the system hard to understand
quiz.explain: Triggers run invisibly. Too many of them make a database hard to understand and debug.

days.title: Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
days.goal: Write clearer complex queries with WITH and CTEs.

video.title: What a Table Is and Your First SELECT | Six Minutes: SQL, Part 1

steps: Write a query with WITH that names a subquery and uses it twice.
Use a CTE to find the average order value, then list orders above it.
Chain two CTEs: one for totals per customer, one for the top customers.
Compare the CTE version with the subquery version for readability.
days.task: Rewrite your best-selling product query using a CTE.
days.challenge: Use a CTE to find customers who spent more than twice the average.

options: A named temporary result you define with WITH and use like a table in your query
quiz.explain: A CTE is a named query defined with WITH. You can use it in the main query like a table.

quiz.q: Why use a CTE instead of a subquery?
options: It makes complex queries easier to read and lets you reuse the same result twice
quiz.explain: CTEs give a name to a step, so a long query reads like a story instead of nested brackets.

quiz.q: Can a CTE call another CTE?
options: Yes, you can define several CTEs separated by commas and use earlier ones in later ones
quiz.explain: You can chain CTEs: define one, then use it in the next, which breaks a hard query into clear steps.

days.title: Importing and Exporting Data
days.goal: Move data in and out of your database with files.

video.title: Learn SQL for Data Analysis in one hour

steps: Export a table to a CSV file.
Import a CSV file into a new table.
Check the row count after import to confirm nothing was lost.
Export your whole database as a backup file.
days.task: Import a real CSV dataset into a new table and run three queries on it.
days.challenge: Export your shop database and restore it under a different name.

quiz.q: Why import data from CSV files?
options: Because real data often arrives as spreadsheets or exports from other systems
quiz.explain: Real-world data comes as CSVs from other tools. Importing brings it into your database so you can query it.

quiz.q: What should you check after an import?
options: The row count, the column types and a few sample rows
quiz.explain: After importing, check the row count matches and the data looks right. Imports can silently drop or misread rows.

quiz.q: What is the simplest way to back up a whole database?
options: Export it to a file with the database's dump tool
quiz.explain: A dump exports the whole database, tables and data, to a file you can restore from later.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your Database Project
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone project and plan your demo.

video.title: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners

steps: List the databases you built and pick the most interesting one.
Write a short plan: the business, the tables, the relationships and the report.
Practise explaining your design in simple words, as if to a friend.
Record a short video or write a short post showing your database and report.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your database.
days.challenge: Show your report to one person and note their questions, then improve it.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone database?
options: A real business problem, clean design, realistic data and a useful report
quiz.explain: A good capstone solves a real problem with clean tables, realistic data and a report someone can use.

options: Because explaining simply proves you truly understand it
quiz.explain: If you can explain your design in simple words, you really understand it. That is what employers look for.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The business, the tables, the relationships, the report and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the business problem, the tables and links, the report queries and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Design and Build a Business Database with Reports
capstone.brief: Design and build a complete database for a real small business: a shop, a school, a clinic or a gym. It must have at least five tables with correct relationships, realistic data, indexes on the columns you filter on, two views, and a written report with queries that answer real business questions. Present it with a short demo.
checks: The database solves a real business problem and you can explain the business in one sentence.
It has at least five tables with primary and foreign keys.
It includes a many-to-many relationship with a join table.
The tables hold realistic data (at least 30 rows in the main tables).
Indexes exist on the columns the report filters and joins on.
Two views exist and the report uses them.
You can present the design and the report in under five minutes in simple words.
deliverables: A working database (the SQL file that creates it).
A diagram or written description of the tables and relationships.
A written report with at least five queries and findings.
A short demo video or screenshots showing the queries running.
A one-page write-up of what you learned in 30 days.
